lines.text: Today your programs start to listen. You will store answers in variables and use them in a funny story.
A variable stores a value under a name, like score = 0.
The = sign means “put this value in the box”.
Later you can use the name instead of the value.
input("What is your name? ") shows a question and waits for the user to type.
Whatever they type is stored, usually in a variable. input() always gives back text, even if they type a number.
Put an f before the quotes and a variable name inside curly brackets.
So f"Hi {name}!" becomes Hi Meera! when name holds Meera.
Names can use letters, numbers and underscores, but cannot start with a number or have spaces.
Choose names that explain themselves, like player_name or total_runs.
We put the text Mumbai Waves into a variable called team.
Now we can use the word team again and again, without typing the whole name.
A variable holds one value at a time.
When we store vada pav, the samosa is replaced, so only vada pav is printed.
The input command shows the question and waits for the user to type.
Riya typed her name, and the f-string dropped it straight into the sentence.
Oops, the output says curly bracket name instead of Kabir.
We forgot the little f before the quotes, so Python printed the brackets as plain text.
Great work! Let’s remember what we learned.
Now build along, then try the challenges. You’ve got this!
